Results Summary: AGP Dataset
text:
In this script 4 models are considered: 3 already used in the previous scripts, namely: logistic regression with L1 penalty, Random Forest and XGBoost. The fourth used model is the sparse log-contrast classification model as implemented in the R package trac version 0.0.2 (see viettr/trac GitHub repository for the implementation details).
Sparse log-contrast classification model with square hinge loss: The model can be described as follows: \[
y = X \beta + \sigma \epsilon \quad \text{subject to} \quad C \beta = 0
\]
where \(y\) is a binary outcome vector, \(X\) is a predictor matrix, \(C\) is a general constraint matrix, \(\beta\) is an unknown coefficient vector and \(\sigma\) is an unknown scale parameter. In this analysis the squared hinge loss is used with an \(\ell_1\) penalty for the \(\beta\) coefficients. Therefore, the optimization problem is defined as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{d}}
\quad & \sum_{i=1}^{n} \, \ell\!\left(y_i\, x_i^{\top}\beta\right) \;+\; \lambda \lVert \beta \rVert_{1} \\
\text{subject to}\quad & C\beta = 0 ,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the \(x_i\) are the rows of \(X\), \(\lVert \beta \rVert_{1}\) is the \(\ell_1\) penalty and the loss function \(\ell(\cdot)\) is defined as:
\[
\ell(r)=
\begin{cases}
(1-r)^2, & \text{if } r \le 1,\\[4pt]
0, & \text{if } r \ge 1.
\end{cases}
\]
Given this setup, the fitted model outputs a score for each observation, which can be thresholded to obtain class predictions. To obtain probabilities, an additional step is required (e.g., additional model transforming scores into probabilities). Consequently, Brier scores are not reported for the sparse log-contrast models.

title: Density Impact
text:
The purpose of this document is to show the influence of the density of a skew-symmetric matrix used for a generation of a GHL matrix used in the random ILR augmentation methods.
Reminder: Density \(\delta=0.1\) means that \(10\%\) of the off-diagonal entries in the skew-symmetric matrix \(S\) are non-zero; each such non-zero value is drawn from a standard normal distribution (\(s_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\)) and \(s_{ji}=-s_{ij}\). The default density refers to the very sparse case in which exactly one off-diagonal element in the lower triangle and its mirror element in the upper triangle are non-zero; all other off-diagonal entries are zero.
To understand the impact of density of skew-symmetric matrix on the GHL matrix, and in consequence on the random ilr transformation, one needs to understand first in terms of the formulas how is the GHL matrix used in the random ilr transformation. In order to achieve it, let’s have a look on the below example with the use of the four dimensional compositional vector \(\mathbf{x},\, \mathbf{x} \in S^4\):
\[
\mathbf{x} \in S^{4}, \; \mathbf{x}=\bigl[\,x_{1},\,x_{2},\,x_{3},\,x_{4}\,\bigr]
\]
\[
\mathrm{ilr}(x)=\mathrm{clr}(x)\,\mathrm{L}_{-1}=\bigl[\,y_{1},\,y_{2},\,y_{3}\,\bigr],
\]
where \(L_{-1}\) is the GHL matrix without last column and \(dim\bigl(L_{-1}\bigr) = 4 \times 3\). The centered log-ratio transformation is given by:
\[
\mathrm{clr}(x)=\Bigl[\,\ln\frac{x_{1}}{g(x)},\,\ln\frac{x_{2}}{g(x)},\,\ln\frac{x_{3}}{g(x)},\,\ln\frac{x_{4}}{g(x)}\,\Bigr],
\]
where \(g(x)\) is a geometric mean of the entries of a vector \(\mathbf{x}\) . Let’s represent the GHL matrix with the removed last column as follows:
\[
L_{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}a_{1} & b_{1} & c_{1} \\a_{2} & b_{2} & c_{2} \\a_{3} & b_{3} & c_{3} \\a_{4} & b_{4} & c_{4}\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{ilr}(x)&=\mathrm{clr}(x)\,\mathrm{L}_{-1} \\
&=\Bigl[\,a_{1}\ln\frac{x_{1}}{g(x)}+a_{2}\ln\frac{x_{2}}{g(x)}+a_{3}\ln\frac{x_{3}}{g(x)}+a_{4}\ln\frac{x_{4}}{g(x)},\;\\ & \,b_{1}\ln\frac{x_{1}}{g(x)}+b_{2}\ln\frac{x_{2}}{g(x)}+b_{3}\ln\frac{x_{3}}{g(x)}+b_{4}\ln\frac{x_{4}}{g(x)}, \;\\
& \,c_{1}\ln\frac{x_{1}}{g(x)}+c_{2}\ln\frac{x_{2}}{g(x)}+c_{3}\ln\frac{x_{3}}{g(x)}+c_{4}\ln\frac{x_{4}}{g(x)},
\Bigr] \\
&=\Biggl[\,\ln\frac{x_{1}^{a_{1}}x_{2}^{a_{2}}x_{3}^{a_{3}}x_{4}^{a_{4}}}{\bigl[g(x)\bigr]^{a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}}},\; \ln\frac{x_{1}^{b_{1}}x_{2}^{b_{2}}x_{3}^{b_{3}}x_{4}^{b_{4}}}{\bigl[g(x)\bigr]^{b_{1}+b_{2}+b_{3}+b_{4}}},\;
\ln\frac{x_{1}^{c_{1}}x_{2}^{c_{2}}x_{3}^{c_{3}}x_{4}^{c_{4}}}{\bigl[g(x)\bigr]^{c_{1}+c_{2}+c_{3}+c_{4}}}
\Biggr] \\
&= \Bigl[\,\ln\!\bigl(x_{1}^{a_{1}}x_{2}^{a_{2}}x_{3}^{a_{3}}x_{4}^{a_{4}}\bigr),\;
\ln\!\bigl(x_{1}^{b_{1}}x_{2}^{b_{2}}x_{3}^{b_{3}}x_{4}^{b_{4}}\bigr),\;
\ln\!\bigl(x_{1}^{c_{1}}x_{2}^{c_{2}}x_{3}^{c_{3}}x_{4}^{c_{4}}\bigr)
\Bigr]
\end{aligned}
\]
The last equality in the above representation of the random ilr transformation is the consequence of the following property of GHL matrix under consideration:
\[
\mathbf{1}_{n}^{\mathsf T}L_{n,n-1}=\mathbf{0}_{n-1}^{\mathsf T}
\]
therefore: \(a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=0\). Similarly for \(b_{i}, c_{i}, i \in \{1,2,3,4\}\). Therefore, the contribution of a original feature \(x_i\) to the new coordinate after random ilr transformation (\(y_i\)) depends on the sign of coefficients from GHL matrix \(a_i, b_i, c_i, i \in \{1, \dots, 4\}\). For instance, in the considered example of \(\mathbf{x}, \, \mathbf{x} \in S^4\) let’s focus on the first coordinate resulting from the random ilr transformation. Let’s assume that \(a_1, a_3 > 0\) and \(a_2, a_4 <0\). Then, the new first ilr coordinate has the following form:
\[
y_{1}=\ln\!\left(\frac{x_{1}^{a_{1}}\,x_{3}^{a_{3}}}{x_{2}^{a_{2}}\,x_{4}^{a_{4}}}\right)
\]
In such a case original features \(x_1, x_3\) contribute to the new coordinate in the numerator, while covariates \(x_2, x_4\) contribute to the \(y_1\) in the denominator.
The strength of the contribution of a given original feature to the new random ilr coordinate depends on the absolute value of the coefficient from the GHL matrix. For example, the contribution of \(x_1\) to ilr coordinate \(y_1\) depends on the \(|a_1|\). In the below analysis term top k contributor will be used.
Top k contributor: Feature \(x_j\) coming from compositional vector \(\mathbf{x}, \, \mathbf{x} \in S^p\) is considered as the top \(k\) contributor to the new ilr coordinate \(y_i, \, y_i = \ln\!\bigl(x_{1}^{w_{1}}x_{2}^{w_{2}} \dots x_{p}^{w_{p}}\bigr) \; \text{where} \; \mathbf{y} = \bigl(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{p-1} \bigr)\) when the absolute value of the coefficient from GHL matrix associated with \(x_j\) ranks within top \(k\) largest absolute coefficients \(|w_1|, |w_2|, \dots, |w_p|\).

title: Density Impact
text:
Analysis
Helper functions used in this script:


Code
# Function that takes the GHL matrix and:
# 1. determines if original feature x_i contributes to the ilr coordinate in numerator or denominator
# 2. determines top k contributors for each of the
understand_randilr <- function(ghl, org_feature_names, top_k) {
    abs_ghl <- abs(ghl)
    sign_ghl <- sign(ghl)

    ghl_summary <- map(c(1:ncol(ghl)), function(j) {
        # Pull the j-th column
        abs_col <- abs_ghl[, j]
        sign_col <- sign_ghl[, j]
        column <- ghl[, j]

        # Get names of the original features that go into numerator (have positive 'coefficient' in the GHL mat.):
        pos <- org_feature_names[sign_col == 1]
        # Get names of the original features that go into denominator
        neg <- org_feature_names[sign_col == -1]

        # top-k absolute contributors and the values of their coeffs (not absolute, just as is)
        idx <- order(abs_col, decreasing = TRUE)[1:top_k]
        top_k_tbl <- tibble(
            feature = org_feature_names[idx],
            coef    = column[idx]
        )

        # number of distinct absolute values of coeff
        unique_coefs <- length(unique(abs_col))

        list(
            column = j,
            unique_coefs = unique_coefs,
            numerator = pos,
            denominator = neg,
            top_k_contribution = top_k_tbl
        )
    })

    # Return tibble
    tibble(
        column = map_dbl(ghl_summary, ~ .x$column),
        unique_coefs = map_dbl(ghl_summary, ~ .x$unique_coefs),
        numerator = map(ghl_summary, ~ .x$numerator),
        denominator = map(ghl_summary, ~ .x$denominator),
        top_contribution = map(ghl_summary, ~ .x$top_k_contribution)
    )
}

# Function:
# 1. Construct square GHL matrix with n_org_features rows and column by using skew-symmetric matrix with `density`
# 2. Gathers info about contribution to numerator/denominator of each feature and top k contributors
# 3. repeats 1-2 n_iters times
density_impact <- function(seed_start = 2025, n_org_features, density, top_k, n_iters = 10) {
    set.seed(seed_start)
    org_feature_names <- paste0("org_feature", c(1:n_org_features))
    results <- tibble()

    for (i in 1:n_iters) {
        # Generate GHL matrix
        ghl <- create_ghl(n = n_org_features, density = density)
        ghl_mat <- ghl[, -n_org_features]

        # Gather info about new features
        out <- understand_randilr(
            ghl = ghl_mat,
            org_feature_names = org_feature_names,
            top_k = top_k
        ) |>
            mutate(iter = i)

        results <- results |>
            bind_rows(out)
    }
    return(results)
}


In the below analysis the following scenario is considered:

input data has \(20\) covariates,
analyzed density of skew-symmetric matrix : default density (very sparse skew-symmetric matrix) and \(\delta \in (0.01, 0.02, \dots, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, \dots, 0.9)\),
for each density level of a skew-symmetric matrix, \(100\) independent GHL matrices are generated,
for a given GHL matrix, the proportion of times when a given original feature contributes to the numerator vs. denominator along with the top \(5\) contributors are analyzed.


Contribution to numerator vs denominator

    ) |>

title: Random ILR Thesis
text:
The purpose of this page is to summarise the results of the experiments and provide recommendations for the use of augmentation techniques.Before that, explanations of frequently used terms are provided.

Definitions

Pseudo-count (PC): a small numeric value added to all numeric entries in the dataset (in our case, “species” counts). In this project two pseudo-counts are considered: 0.5 and 1/max library size (the maximum row sum in a given dataset). After adding the pseudo-count, data are converted to proportions. The motivation to use a pseudo-count is that non-zero entries are required by definition by all random ILR augmentation methods and by the Aitchison augmentation strategy (due to its implementation).
Random ILR augmentation methods — unit vs relative density: to apply any random ILR augmentation technique, a Generalised Helmert–Ledermann (GHL) orthogonal matrix is first constructed, which requires a skew-symmetric matrix. Density refers to the fraction of off-diagonal entries (e.g., in the lower triangle) that are set to non-zero when constructing the skew-symmetric matrix. The naming convention, referring to the skew-symmetric matrix used in the Cayley transform (which in turn is used to generate the GHL matrix), is as follows:

Unit density: exactly one off-diagonal pair of entries \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\) in the \(S_{n−1}\) skew-symmetric matrix is non-zero, independent of the matrix size \(n\).
Relative density: the number of non-zero off-diagonal elements is a fixed proportion of all off-diagonal elements (equivalently, of the elements in one triangle). For example, for a \(5 \times 5\) skew-symmetric matrix there are \(10\) entries in each triangle. If the density is \(0.2\), then \(20\%\) of off-diagonal entries are set to non-zero (so in our example it would be \(2\) out of \(10\) entries). The term “relative density” indicates that the exact count of non-zero off-diagonal entries scales with the matrix size.

Definitions of performance metrics analysed throughout the experiments:

ROC AUC: the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve.
Misclassification Rate = 1 − accuracy, where accuracy is the proportion of observations predicted correctly. Thus, misclassification rate is the proportion of observations predicted incorrectly by the classification model.




Results Overview: Random ILR and Rodriguez Augmentation Methods
The conclusions drawn below are heavily based on the results obtained in the “Methods comparison” dashboard.

Logistic regression with L1 penalty:

Across both pseudo-counts and all augmentation factors, a one of random ILR method most often achieves the best test ROC AUC and misclassification rate.
In the n/p ratio vs. performance plots, small values of n/p ratios show larger variability (both gains and losses) in the performance. As n/p increases, the impact of any augmentation method tends toward zero.
For small values of n/p ratio and when using misclassification rate as the perfromance metric, methods from the random ILR group show a clear performance gain over their benchmarks.

Random Forest:

Pseudo-count 1/2: ROC AUC is slightly more often higher with one of the Rodriguez methods, whereas a lower misclassification rate is more often achieved by one of the random ILR methods.
Pseudo-count 1/max library size: For both metrics, Rodriguez methods more often lead to better perfromance.
Task 1: For both metrics and both pseudo-counts, augmentation in p (any relative density) consistently outperforms the Rodriguez methods.
Tasks 10 and 12 (ROC AUC): Almost all random ILR methods consistently outperform the Rodriguez techniques.
Relation between n/p ratio and the performance gain- in general bigger variability in gain for small values of n/p ratio, with growing value of n/p ratio the gain tends towards zero. Independently of the analysed perfromance metric there is the biggest possible gain is for the datasets with small n/p ratio when using Rodriguez or random ILR augmentation in p.
Relationship between the n/p ratio and performance gain: in general, variability in gain is larger for small n/p values, and as n/p increases the gain tends toward zero. Regardless of the performance metric, the biggest possible perfromance gain occurs for datasets with small n/p when using Rodriguez methods or random ILR augmentation in p.

XGBoost:

A Rodriguez method most often yields the best performance across both pseudo-counts and both metrics.
Visual inspection of the heatmaps suggests that performance varies slightly less across augmentation techniques than for Random Forest or logistic regression with L1 penalty.
As for two otehr models, for small values of n/p ratio the variability of perfromance gains is the biggest and tends towards zero as the value of n/p increases. Compared to RF and logistic regression, the variability for small values of n/p ratio seems to be small.
As with the other models, performance gains are most variable at small n/p ratio and tend toward zero as n/p increases. However, the variability in the perfromance gain for small n/p values appears smaller for XGBoost than for Random Forest or L1-logistic regression.


General conclusions:

If one wants to use random ILR augmentation, then independent of the objective (the performance measure to optimize) I would recommend augmentation in p as it outperforms augmentation in n in my experiments.
Impact of augmentation factor: Across the pseudo-counts, augmentation techniques, and performance metrics considered, model performance was fairly stable across all analyzed augmentation factors.
Sensitivity to pseudo-count: Across augmentation factors and techniques, for L1-penalized logistic regression a pseudo-count of 0.5 more often led to better performance, whereas for XGBoost and Random Forest a pseudo-count of 1/max library size more often yielded better-performing models. However, the performance differences between pseudo-counts are subtle in the majority of cases.
Impact of density in the random ILR augmentation in p: For both performance metrics and pseudo-count = 0.5, across all considered models, relative densities (0.1 or 0.5) more often led to better performance than numeric densities. For pseudo-count = 1/max library size, Random Forest still favored relative densities for both ROC AUC and misclassification rate, whereas for logistic regression with L1 penalty and XGBoost, unit density seemed to be the better choice. In general, the performance differences between densities are not large, so the density should be treated as a tunable parameter. I recommend focusing on relative densities rather than unit density, as in my experience they usually yield better results.

To which tasks augmentation is most beneficial:

L1-penalized logistic regression: for both performance metrics with pseudo-count = 1/max library size, starting from augmentation factor 3, tasks 7, 8, and 9 benefit more from random ILR augmentation than from the Rodriguez strategies. With pseudo-count = 1/2, tasks 8 and 9 generally benefit from random ILR augmentation, whereas for task 2 a gain in ROC AUC is observed only for augmentation in p.
Random Forest: across all performance metrics and pseudo-counts, augmentation in n generally worsens performance. For both metrics with pseudo-count = 1/2, tasks 1, 8, 10, and 12 show benefits from random ILR augmentation in p with relative density as compared to Rodriguez methods, but the effect tends to diminish as the augmentation factor increases.
XGBoost: across augmentation factors and performance metrics, Rodriguez techniques generally outperform random ILR methods. Only for task 4 augmentation in n with unit density consistently leads to higher perfromance than any Rodriguez augmentation methd. However, compared with the other two models, the difference between the two augmentation groups appears smallest for XGBoost.

title: Results Summary: Lupus Dataset
text:
In this script 4 models are considered: 3 already used in the previous scripts, namely: logistic regression with L1 penalty, Random Forest and XGBoost. The fourth used model is the sparse log-contrast classification model as implemented in the R package trac version 0.0.2 (see viettr/trac GitHub repository for the implementation details).
Sparse log-contrast classification model with square hinge loss: The model can be described as follows: \[
y = X \beta + \sigma \epsilon \quad \text{subject to} \quad C \beta = 0
\]
where \(y\) is a binary outcome vector, \(X\) is a predictor matrix, \(C\) is a general constraint matrix, \(\beta\) is an unknown coefficient vector and \(\sigma\) is an unknown scale parameter. In this analysis the squared hinge loss is used with an \(\ell_1\) penalty for the \(\beta\) coefficients. Therefore, the optimization problem is defined as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{d}}
\quad & \sum_{i=1}^{n} \, \ell\!\left(y_i\, x_i^{\top}\beta\right) \;+\; \lambda \lVert \beta \rVert_{1} \\
\text{subject to}\quad & C\beta = 0 ,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the \(x_i\) are the rows of \(X\), \(\lVert \beta \rVert_{1}\) is the \(\ell_1\) penalty and the loss function \(\ell(\cdot)\) is defined as:
\[
\ell(r)=
\begin{cases}
(1-r)^2, & \text{if } r \le 1,\\[4pt]
0, & \text{if } r \ge 1.
\end{cases}
\]
Given this setup, the fitted model outputs a score for each observation, which can be thresholded to obtain class predictions. To obtain probabilities, an additional step is required (e.g., additional model transforming scores into probabilities). Consequently, Brier scores are not reported for the sparse log-contrast models.
